elements.quote: Worldwide, surgery related deaths within 30 days of the procedure accounts the third contributor among all causes of deaths, with an estimated 4.2 million people annually and half of these deaths occur in low and middle income countries.
elements.reason: Provides a brief statement of the global burden of surgical-related deaths, giving some context for the topic, but does not clearly describe the current state of knowledge or explicitly identify important uncertainties specific to surgical site infection after cesarean section in Ethiopia.

elements.quote: Wehave checked the PROSPERO database https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/displayrecord.php?) to see whether recently published or ongoing projects exist related to the topic to avoid any further unnecessary duplication: This systematic review and meta-analysis were registered in the PROSPERO database with ID no. CRD42023442583. A SRMA was conducted on SSI following cesarean section and its predictors in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: Explicitly states that the authors checked for existing projects to avoid duplication and registered the review, and declares that the SRMA was conducted on SSI following cesarean section and its predictors in Ethiopia, which explains the importance/need for the current review.

elements.quote: Wehave checked the PROSPERO database ... to see whether recently published or ongoing projects exist related to the topic to avoid any further unnecessary duplication: This systematic review and meta-analysis were registered in the PROSPERO database with ID no. CRD42023442583.
elements.reason: The authors report searching PROSPERO to identify existing or ongoing reviews and state the registration of their review, addressing the need for the current review in the context of similar work.
This review addresses prevalence and predictors of surgical site infection (observational studies), not effects of interventions; no mechanism of action of an intervention is relevant or reported.
The review does not evaluate complex interventions or delivery contexts and no logic model is relevant or reported.

elements.quote: To determine the pooled prevalence of SSI following cesarean section and its predictors in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides an explicit objective statement describing the review's aims (pooled prevalence and predictors). However, the objective is not presented using a formal question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO or an equivalent), so it only partially meets the requirement.

elements.quote: This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs were included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: The conditional item applies to reviews of intervention effects. This review is a prevalence and predictors SRMA of observational studies (not intervention effects), so specification of planned comparisons using PICO is not applicable.

elements.quote: This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs (case-control and cross-sectional study designs) were included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies eligible settings (all regional states of Ethiopia) and eligible study designs (observational: case-control and cross-sectional) and the outcomes of interest (prevalence/incidence and associated factors). It does not specify follow-up requirements or other question-framework components (e.g., participant characteristics, timing/follow-up), so the eligibility characteristics are incompletely reported.

elements.quote: Both published articles and grey literatures published in English language from January 1 2013 to September 2023.
elements.reason: The review states report characteristics: inclusion of published and grey literature, restriction to English language, and the dissemination years (January 1, 2013 to September 2023).

The manuscript states that "Articles which lack our outcome of interest... were excluded," but does not distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Based on the study region, subgroup analyses were done.
elements.reason: The review specifies one way studies were grouped for synthesis (subgroup analyses by study region). However, it does not comprehensively specify all groups used for each synthesis or explicitly link these groups to the comparisons defined in the review objectives, so reporting is partial.
No rationale is provided in the retrieved text for notable restrictions on eligibility (for example, the reason for the 2013–2023 date range or English-language restriction is not given).

elements.quote: The electronic literature search was last performed on September 23, 2023.
elements.reason: A search date is reported for the electronic literature search overall, but the date on which each individual information source was last searched or consulted is not provided.

elements.quote: An appropriate and comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Google Scholar, HINARI and Scopus was done.
elements.reason: Database names are listed but no search interface/platform (e.g., Ovid, EBSCOhost) or coverage dates for each database are reported.

elements.quote: Wehave checked the PROSPERO database https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/displayrecord.php?) to see whether recently published or ongoing projects exist related to the topic to avoid any further unnecessary duplication: This systematic review and meta-analysis were registered in the PROSPERO database with ID no. CRD42023442583.
elements.reason: A study register (PROSPERO) is named and a registration ID/URL is provided, but no information on any date restrictions applied when searching the register is reported.

elements.quote: An appropriate and comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Google Scholar, HINARI and Scopus was done since 2013.
elements.reason: Some online sources/search engines are named (e.g., Google Scholar, HINARI) and PROSPERO URL is given elsewhere, but URLs are not provided for each website/search engine and not all online sources have accompanying URLs.
No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies; no organisations are named as contacted.
No description is provided of types of individuals (e.g., experts, authors) contacted to identify studies.
The manuscript does not specify the types of reference lists examined (e.g., bibliographies of included studies, systematic reviews).
No information is provided about backward or forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index or platform, or search date).
No journals or conference proceedings are named as consulted, nor are dates covered or search methods for such sources reported.

elements.quote: An appropriate and comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Google Scholar, HINARI and Scopus was done since 2013. ... Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and key terms had been developed using different Boolean operators 'AND' and 'OR'. The following search terms were used: '(prevalence) OR (magnitude) OR (proportion) OR (epidemiology) OR (surgical site infection) OR (surgical site) OR (wound infection) AND (cesarean section) OR (cesarean delivery) OR (post cesarean section) AND (determinants) OR (associated factors) OR (risk factors) OR (predictors) AND (Ethiopia)'. The electronic literature search was last performed on September 23, 2023.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports databases searched, a combined search string and the date of the last search, but does not provide the complete, database-specific search strategies as actually run (e.g., exact PubMed, Embase, Scopus queries with field tags, limits, or syntax variations).

elements.quote: Eligible literatures in English language only were identified. ... An appropriate and comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Google Scholar, HINARI and Scopus was done since 2013.
elements.reason: The manuscript states language (English only) and a start year (since 2013) as limits, but does not describe or justify these limits with reference to the eligibility criteria in detail.
No citation or description of published search approaches or filters and no description of any adaptations is provided in the available evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms is present in the provided evidence.
There is no information about tools used to translate search strings between sources in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence contains no description of any validation of the search strategy or related validation studies/processes.
No description of peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or the process/tool used is present in the provided text.

Although MeSH and Boolean terms are mentioned, there is no statement that the search structure was not based on PICO nor a description of an alternative conceptual structure or explorations used to develop the search.

No explicit statement reporting the number of reviewers who screened records and full reports at each screening stage. The evidence describes who searched and who extracted data, but does not state how many reviewers screened titles/abstracts or full texts.

No explicit information on whether reviewers worked independently at each screening stage. The text states two authors searched and two authors independently extracted data, but does not state independence of title/abstract or full-text screening.

elements.quote: Any disagreement between reviewers was resolved by the third author (AA). Consensus was declared through critical discussion and evaluation of the articles by all the independent reviewers.
elements.reason: Describes the process used to resolve screening/disagreement: involvement of a third author (AA) and resolution by discussion and consensus.
No description of processes used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators (no evidence of contacting authors or procedures to obtain additional information).

elements.quote: Eligible literatures in English language only were identified.
elements.reason: The review restricted inclusion to English-language studies, so methods for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment do not apply.

elements.quote: All the datasets were exported to Mendeley reference manager, and then we transferred to the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet to remove duplicate data in the review.
elements.reason: Describes use of Mendeley and Excel to manage records and remove duplicates, indicating integration of these tools into the selection process (duplicate removal).
No evidence that externally derived classifiers were used to remove records prior to screening; nothing reported about such classifiers or removed records in the flow diagram.
No evidence that internally derived classifiers were used; no description of training, validation, or use of such classifiers.
No evidence of machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules being used in the selection process.
No evidence that crowdsourcing platforms were used or integrated into study selection.
No evidence that previously screened datasets were used to eliminate records; nothing reported about using such datasets or how they were derived.

elements.quote: Two authors (ES and MA) independently extracted all the important data using standardized data extraction format developed according to 2014 Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Reviewers' manual [24].
elements.reason: Explicitly states the number of reviewers (two authors ES and MA) who collected/extracted data from reports.

elements.quote: Two authors (ES and MA) independently extracted all the important data using standardized data extraction format developed according to 2014 Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Reviewers' manual [24].
elements.reason: Specifies that the two data collectors worked independently.

elements.quote: Any disagreement between reviewers was resolved by the third author (AA). Consensus was declared through critical discussion and evaluation of the articles by all the independent reviewers.
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving disagreements (involvement of a third author AA and consensus via discussion).
No information provided about processes to obtain or confirm data from study investigators in the supplied evidence.
No description of automation tools used for data collection, their use, training, or validation is present in the provided evidence.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No software for extracting data from figures is specified in the provided text.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies between reports are described in the available evidence.

elements.quote: This SRMA has comprised of two main outcomes. The primary outcome was magnitude of SSI among women underwent cesarean section, which is defined as the proportion of women after cesarean section who fulfills the CDC criteria of surgical site definition within 30 days of post-partum and it could be at least one of the following: ( A superficial incisional , deep incisional or deep/organ SSI) . The secondary outcome was the determinants of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines the primary outcome (magnitude of SSI, including CDC definitions and SSI types) and the secondary outcome (determinants).

elements.quote: which is defined as the proportion of women after cesarean section who fulfills the CDC criteria of surgical site definition within 30 days of post-partum
elements.reason: The time frame for the primary outcome is explicitly specified as within 30 days postpartum.
There is no statement indicating whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g. all measures, time points, analyses) were sought across included studies.

elements.quote: Two authors (ES and MA) independently extracted all the important data using standardized data extraction format developed according to 2014 Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Reviewers' manual [24]. ... The name of the author, sample size, publication year, study region, study design, prevalence/proportion of surgical site infection, and adjusted odds ratio with its 95% CI of the factors associated with SSI.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process and specific data elements extracted (e.g. prevalence/proportion and adjusted ORs), indicating how results were selected for extraction when collecting data.
No information is provided about any changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance, nor rationales for such changes.
No information is provided about any changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.
The manuscript does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions nor provide rationale for any prioritisation.

elements.quote: The name of the author, sample size, publication year, study region, study design, prevalence/proportion of surgical site infection, and adjusted odds ratio with its 95% CI of the factors associated with SSI.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the other variables for which data were sought (author name, sample size, year, region, study design, prevalence/proportion of SSI, and adjusted ORs with 95% CIs).
No text in the provided evidence describes any assumptions made about missing or unclear study information.

elements.quote: Two authors (ES and MA) independently extracted all the important data using standardized data extraction format developed according to 2014 Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Reviewers' manual [24].
elements.reason: The authors cite the JBI Reviewers' Manual and state they used a standardized data extraction format developed according to it, indicating a named tool/guidance used to determine data items to collect.

elements.quote: we used Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment scale (NOS) adapted for observational studies to assess the quality of each study included in this SRMA [25] (S1 Table).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly names the risk-of-bias tool used (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, adapted for observational studies).

elements.quote: This quality assessment scale evaluates the literatures in three categories: Selection (4 points) Comparability(2points) and Outcome (3 points)
elements.reason: The domains/components of the NOS used are specified (Selection, Comparability, Outcome with point allocations).

elements.quote: On the other hand, the quality of each study was assessed by using NOS, the score of all included studies lies between 8 to 9 which indicates good quality (Table 1) (1).
elements.reason: An overall judgment (studies scored 8–9 and described as 'good quality') is reported, but the explicit rules or thresholds used to derive that overall risk-of-bias judgement (e.g., cutoffs or how domain ratings map to overall judgment) are not fully described.

elements.quote: we used Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment scale (NOS) adapted for observational studies to assess the quality of each study included in this SRMA [25] (S1 Table).
elements.reason: The manuscript states the NOS was 'adapted for observational studies', but it does not describe what adaptations were made or provide details of the modifications.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool was reported; an existing tool (NOS) was used.

elements.quote: Two Authors (ES and MA) assessed the quality of each study (i.e. methodological quality, sample selection, sample size, comparability and the outcome, and statistical analysis of the study). In the case of disagreement between two authors; another third author (AA, WS and BB) were involved and discussed and resolved the disagreement.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (two), that they assessed studies (stated as assessment roles), that they worked independently (implied by 'in the case of disagreement' and consistent with independent assessment elsewhere), and the disagreement-resolution procedure (involving a third author) are reported.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes to obtain/confirm risk-of-bias information from original study authors.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are reported in the available evidence.

elements.quote: A random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI. Adjusted Odds Ratio (OR) with 95% Confidence Interval (CI) was also considered to determine the association of identified variables with SSI.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state the effect measures used: pooled prevalence (via random-effects model) for the primary outcome and adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs for associations.
No thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect sizes (e.g., what constitutes small/large effect) or any rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
No methods for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., converting ORs to risk ratios) are described in the supplied text.
No justification for the choice of effect measures (pooled prevalence or adjusted OR) is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Inclusion. This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs (case-control and cross-sectional study designs) were included in this SRMA. Both published articles and grey literatures published in English language from January 1 2013 to September 2023. Exclusion. which lack our outcome of interest: SSI following cesarean section and its predictors were excluded from this SRMA. On the other hand, literatures with poor quality as per the criteria of reviewing articles were excluded from this SRMA.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies inclusion and exclusion criteria for studies (population, outcomes, study designs, date and language limits) which indicates how studies were deemed eligible for the review generally. However, it does not explicitly describe the processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each specific synthesis (e.g., how studies were matched to particular outcome syntheses or grouped for analyses), nor details on tabulating intervention/characteristic comparisons for each synthesis.

The provided evidence describes data extraction, deduplication, software used (STATA v17), and that adjusted ORs with 95% CIs were used, but does not describe any methods for preparing data for presentation or synthesis such as handling missing summary statistics or specific data conversions.

elements.quote: The name of the author, sample size, publication year, study region, study design, prevalence/proportion of surgical site infection, and adjusted odds ratio with its 95% CI of the factors associated with SSI.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the data fields extracted and therefore the data included in tables (author, sample size, year, region, design, prevalence, AOR with 95% CI), which defines the tabular structure used to display results.

elements.quote: Funnel plot and Eggers test were done to assess publication bias. ... A forest plot format was used to present the pooled prevalence of surgical site infection after cesarean section with 95% CI. To identify determinant factors, we used the pooled AOR in forest plot format with its respective 95%CI.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the graphical methods used: funnel plot and Egger's test for publication bias and forest plots to present pooled prevalence and pooled AORs.

elements.quote: Subgroup analysis was done based on the study region.
elements.reason: The basis for grouping studies is reported: studies were grouped for subgroup analysis by study region (as also shown in the forest-plot subgroup table).

elements.quote: A forest plot format was used to present the pooled prevalence of surgical site infection after cesarean section with 95% CI. Funnel plot and Eggers test were done to assess publication bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports use of standard graphs (forest plots, funnel plot, Egger's test) and does not report use of any non-standard graphs; therefore a rationale for non-standard graphs does not apply.

elements.quote: Statistical analysis was conducted using STATA version 17 software.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the software and version used for statistical synthesis (STATA version 17).
A meta-analysis was performed in this review (pooled prevalence and pooled AORs), so describing alternative syntheses when meta-analysis was not possible does not apply.

elements.quote: Therefore we have used the random effect model to resolve the issue of heterogeneity between included studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the use of a random-effects model and gives a rationale: to address/resolve substantial heterogeneity among studies.

elements.quote: Then random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: The statistical synthesis method is reported: a random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled prevalence (and pooled AORs are reported elsewhere).

elements.quote: Cochrane Q-test and I 2 statistics were computed to assess heterogeneity among all the studies included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify heterogeneity are explicitly reported (Cochrane Q and I2 statistics).
The manuscript does not report which between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) was used for the random-effects meta-analysis.
The method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect in the random-effects meta-analysis is not specified.
No additional implementation details of the random-effects model (e.g., weighting scheme, continuity corrections) are reported.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed or described in the manuscript, so reporting of priors is not applicable.
The manuscript does not describe methods to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.

elements.quote: Initially 6334 studies were identified and finally 19 studies were found eligible for the analysis.
elements.reason: The review proceeded with meta-analyses (pooled estimates were produced); the manuscript does not report any planned syntheses that were judged impossible, so this reporting item is not applicable.

elements.quote: Based on the study region, subgroup analyses were done. The stability or robustness of the pooled estimates to outliers and the impact of individual studies were assessed using sensitivity analysis.
elements.reason: Explicitly states methods used to explore heterogeneity: subgroup analysis by study region and sensitivity analysis to assess influence of individual studies/outliers.

elements.quote: Subgroup analysis was done by using the study region and the result revealed that the pooled prevalence of SSI cesarean section was highest in Amhara region (12.47%; 95% (CI: 7.33, 17.60%), I 2 = 95.28%, P = 0.00) followed by SNNP region (11.76%; 95% (CI: 10.29, 13.22%), I 2 = 0.00%, P = 0.86).
elements.reason: Reports the factor used for subgroup analysis (study region) and reports factor levels (specific regions with prevalence estimates), but does not state any expected direction of effect modification a priori.
No explicit statement indicating whether analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.

elements.quote: Test of θi = θj: Q(5) = 68.85, p = 0.00
elements.reason: Provides test statistics (Q test and p-values) comparing subgroup heterogeneity (results of tests reported), but does not describe the methods in prose or detail how subgroup effects were compared (only test results are presented).

Meta-analysis was performed and subgroup and sensitivity analyses were used to explore heterogeneity; there is no indication that meta-analysis was unsuitable, so informal methods for that situation do not apply.
No information provided identifying which heterogeneity analyses (if any) were not pre-specified.

elements.quote: The stability or robustness of the pooled estimates to outliers and the impact of individual studies were assessed using sensitivity analysis.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that sensitivity analysis was performed to assess robustness and influence of individual studies (text_16) and further reports that the pooled prevalence was not influenced by a single study (text_21). However, it does not provide detailed information about the specific sensitivity analyses performed (e.g., which studies were omitted, alternative models, or exact procedures), so reporting is incomplete.

No evidence was found indicating whether any sensitivity analyses were not pre-specified or identifying post-hoc sensitivity analyses; the manuscript does not state which analyses were pre-specified versus exploratory.

elements.quote: Funnel plot and Eggers test were done to assess publication bias. The p-value > 0.05 indicated that there was no publication bias.
elements.reason: The methods used to assess risk of bias due to missing results (reporting bias) are described: funnel plot and Egger's (Eggers) test with interpretation threshold (p>0.05).
No information is provided about an existing reporting-bias assessment tool's specific domains/items or how an overall judgement was derived.
There is no description of any adaptations made to an existing reporting-bias tool in the provided evidence.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is described in the manuscript; this conditional item does not apply.
The evidence does not state the number of reviewers, their independence, or procedures for resolving disagreements specifically for the reporting-bias assessment.
No processes for obtaining or confirming information from study investigators relevant to reporting-bias assessment are reported.
No automation tools for reporting-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are described in the provided evidence.
No text specifies a tool/system (e.g., GRADE) or version used to assess certainty/confidence in the body of evidence for an outcome; only study-level quality (NOS) is described.

elements.quote: we used Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment scale (NOS) adapted for observational studies to assess the quality of each study included in this SRMA [25] (S1 Table). This quality assessment scale evaluates the literatures in three categories: Selection (4 points) Comparability(2points) and Outcome (3 points)
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the factors/categories (Selection, Comparability, Outcome) and point allocation of the NOS for assessing study quality, but it does not report factors/criteria used to assess certainty/confidence in the body of evidence for outcomes (e.g., risk of bias across studies, inconsistency, imprecision) or how these were applied to outcome-level certainty.
No decision rules or procedures are described for deriving an overall certainty/confidence level for an outcome or interpretation of certainty levels.
No review-specific certainty considerations, thresholds, or rationales are reported in the provided evidence.
No adaptations to an existing certainty-assessment system are described.

elements.quote: Among the studies included in this SRMA, six studies were in Amhara, four in SNNP region, two in Oromia, two in Addis Ababa, two in Harari, one in Dire Dawa and two in Tigray. Fourteen of the studies were cross sectional, four were cohort and one case control studies. A total of 8755 participants with the smallest 166 to the largest 1069 participants included and found the prevalence which ranges from 6.80 to 25.4% of SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia. On the other hand, the quality of each study was assessed by using NOS, the score of all included studies lies between 8 to 9 which indicates good quality (Table 1) (1).

The manuscript identifies individual contributing studies (author names and years) in tables, thereby specifying which studies contributed to the syntheses.

elements.quote: The finding of this SRMA showed that the pooled prevalence of surgical site infection after cesarean section in Ethiopia was 11.13% (95% CI: 9.29, 12.97%), and there is significant heterogeneity between the studies as evidenced by the Cochrane heterogeneity index (I 2 = 86.80%), P = 0.00. Therefore we have used the random effect model to resolve the issue of heterogeneity between included studies. Moreover, we have considered subgroup analysis as a potential way of addressing heterogeneity. The finding was presented using a forest plot (Fig 2).

elements.quote: The result of this SRMA showed the overall pooled prevalence of SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia was 11.13% with a 95% CI: (9.29, 12.97%), which is much higher than the global prevalence of 5.63% [40]. This result is consistent with a study conducted in Rwanda which is 10.9% [14]. However, this was lower than the study conducted in China [15], Jordan [41] and Ekiti state, Nigeria [13] reported 23.3%, 14.4% and 16.01% respectively. ... On the contrary, our study finding was much higher than the studies conducted in developed nations: Ireland [42], Poland [5], Estonia [10] and Egypt [43] reported 0.63%, 0.5%, 6.2% and 5.34% respectively. ... The finding of this study implies that the optimum level of cesarean section should be done in tandem with the initiatives to reduce post-surgical site infection. This review has also identified the factors associated with SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia. Prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis, prolonged PROM, vertical skin incision, decreased post- operative HGB, repeated vaginal examination and general anesthesia were found to be the independent risk factors of surgical site infection following cesarean section in Ethiopia. Women who had prolonged labor were 3.16 times more likely to develop SSI than their counterparts. The finding was similar with the studies conducted in Cross river state, Nigeria [44] and Egypt [43]. ... Mothers after cesarean section who had chorioanionitis during labor and delivery were about 4.26 times more likely to develop SSI than their counter parts. This study finding was similar with the studies conducted in Estonia [10], Poland [5] and Egypt [43]. ... The finding of this review was consistent with other studies conducted in calabar, Nigeria [44] and Nepal [11]. ... This finding is supported with studies conducted in Poland [5], China [15] and Egypt [43]. ... Repeated digital vaginal examination during labor is found to be independently associated with SSI following cesarean section. The likelihood of developing surgical site infection is 3.8 timely higher than their counterparts. This is consistent with studies conducted in Nepal [11]. ... This study finding is supported by a study conducted in Nigeria [46] and Nepal [47]. This is due to vertical type of skin incision ... The odds of developing SSI after cesarean section among women with general anesthesia were about 1.82 times more likely than spinal anesthesia. This study finding was supported by similar studies conducted in China [49].
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly compares the pooled prevalence and identified risk factors to multiple other studies (global estimates, country-specific studies, and studies supporting each identified predictor), thereby interpreting the results in the context of other relevant evidence.
